Attention connects every word to every earlier word, but it cannot tell what order they came in. This lecture fixes that, and builds attention into a complete language model.

The Transformer Architecture

the architecture from the original paper

A GPT-style model keeps only the right half, and drops its middle attention box, the one with arrows coming in from the left half.

Figure: Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need," NeurIPS 2017.

This is the diagram from the paper that introduced the transformer. You saw it at the start of the course as a picture to recognize. Now we can read almost every box in it.

Start with what we already have. The boxes labeled Multi-Head Attention are the attention we built: queries, keys and values, scores, softmax, and a weighted sum of values. The word Masked means the causal mask, so no word can see a later word.

The rest is what this lecture adds, one piece at a time. Positional Encoding, at the bottom, gives attention a sense of word order. Several heads side by side make it multi-head. Feed Forward is a small neural network applied to each position on its own. Add & Norm are two tricks that keep a deep stack trainable. And N× means the whole block is stacked many times. At the top, Linear and Softmax turn the last vectors into probabilities for the next word, exactly as in the neural language model.

One simplification. The paper's model has two halves because it was built for translation: the left half reads the sentence to translate, and the right half writes the translation. A GPT-style language model keeps only the right half, and drops its middle attention box, the one with arrows coming in from the left half. That decoder-only stack is what we build in this lecture, on a real model trained on Tang poems.

Attention Ignores Word Order

  dog bites man . who is hurt ? the ___          answer: man
  man bites dog . who is hurt ? the ___          answer: dog

  at "the", attention reads the same nine words in both sentences:
    a score uses only two word vectors: the query word and one earlier word
    nothing in a word's vector says where the word is
    same scores  ->  same weights  ->  same weighted sum      (a + b = b + a)

  same vector at "the"  ->  same guess for ___  ->  wrong for one of them

A word's vector says what the word is, not where it is. To attention, a sentence is a bag of words.
Both sentences give the same guess for the blank, so the model cannot get both right.

Here are two sentences with the same words in a different order: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog". Add the same question to both: who is hurt? The answer should be "man" in the first and "dog" in the second.

Now think about what attention does at the word "the", just before the blank. Its query is compared with the key of every earlier word, the scores go through softmax, and the output is a weighted sum of values. Each score uses only two vectors: the query of "the" and the key of one earlier word. And the vector for "dog" is the same whether "dog" comes first or third, because the embedding table has one row for "dog" and nothing else.

So in both sentences, "the" gets the same scores for the same nine words, the same weights, and the same weighted sum. Adding them up in a different order does not change a sum. The vector at "the" is identical, the guess for the blank is identical, and at least one of the two answers must be wrong.

This is the problem we ended attention with. To attention, a sentence is a bag of words: it knows which words are there, but not in what order. Before attention can be the core of a language model, the order has to get into the numbers somehow.

Positional Embeddings

𝐱t=E[wt]+P[t]
  E   one row per word:      what the word is       E[dog] = [ 0.8,  0.5]
  P   one row per position:  where the word is      P[1]   = [ 0.1, -0.3]
                                                    P[3]   = [-0.2,  0.4]

  dog bites man .   dog at position 1:   [0.8, 0.5] + [ 0.1, -0.3]  =  [0.9, 0.2]
  man bites dog .   dog at position 3:   [0.8, 0.5] + [-0.2,  0.4]  =  [0.6, 0.9]

  different vectors  ->  different keys  ->  different scores  ->  different guesses

P is a second table with one row for each position. Each word's vector is its row in E plus the row for its position.
The same word in a different place now has a different vector, so attention can tell the two sentences apart.

The fix is the simplest idea that could work. If a word's vector does not say where the word is, put the position into the vector.

We already have one table, E, with one row for each word in the vocabulary. Now add a second table, P, with one row for each position: a row for position one, a row for position two, and so on, up to the longest input the model accepts. Before anything else happens, each word's vector is its row in E plus the row for its position. That is the Positional Encoding box at the bottom of the diagram.

Follow "dog". In "dog bites man" it is at position one, so its vector is E of dog plus P of one. In "man bites dog" it is at position three, so its vector is E of dog plus P of three. Same word, different place, different vector. Its key is different, so its scores are different, so the vector at "the" is different in the two sentences, and the model can give two different answers.

Where do the rows of P come from? The simplest answer: learn them, exactly like E. They start as random numbers and are adjusted by the same training that adjusts everything else. Nobody tells the model what position three should look like; it finds whatever numbers help it predict the next word.

One consequence of a learned table: it has a fixed number of rows. A model whose table has 1,024 rows has no vector for position 1,025, so it cannot read a longer input. That is one source of the context length you see in model descriptions.

Three Ways to Encode Position

the 2017 paper's formula, shrunk to four numbers per position

P[t]=[sin(t),cos(t),sin(t/100),cos(t/100)]
  position    sin(t)   cos(t)   sin(t/100)   cos(t/100)
     1          0.84     0.54      0.01         1.00
     2          0.91    -0.42      0.02         1.00
     3          0.14    -0.99      0.03         1.00
     4         -0.76    -0.65      0.04         1.00

  learned P    trained, like E                    GPT-2, BERT
  sin and cos  fixed formula, nothing to train    the 2017 Transformer
  RoPE         turn q and k by the position       Llama, Qwen, most open models

The 2017 paper computed each row of P with sines and cosines instead of learning it. Every position gets its own row.
Learned, formula, or rotation: in all three, the position is written into the numbers.

Learning P is not the only way to fill the table, and the original 2017 paper did something else. It computed P with a formula of sines and cosines, so there was nothing to train.

The slide shows the formula shrunk to four numbers per position. To get the row for a position, put the position number t into the formula. Position one gives 0.84, 0.54, 0.01, 1.00. Position two gives 0.91, minus 0.42, 0.02, 1.00. Every position gets a different row, and every number stays between minus one and one, however long the input. The real formula works the same way with more numbers: 512 in the paper.

Why a formula? Nothing has to be trained, and it gives a row for any position, even one longer than any training text. In the paper, a learned table worked about as well, and GPT-2 and BERT went back to learning P.

Most open models today use a third way, called RoPE, for rotary position embedding. Instead of adding a position vector to the word, it turns the query and key vectors by an angle that depends on their position. When a query is compared with a key, what matters is the difference between their two angles, which means how far apart the two words are, not where they are.

Three versions, one idea. Attention cannot see order, so order is written into the numbers.

Multi-Head Attention

  "she gave him the book": what does "gave" need?
    who gave?        she       one head: one softmax shares 100%
    gave to whom?    him       across all three, so its output
    gave what?       book      is a blend of all three
    several heads: each asks one question, each finds one word

  output: heads side by side, then a learned matrix W_O
MultiHead(X)=Concat(head1,…,headh)WO

One head must share its weight between everything a word needs. Several heads each choose separately.
h heads of width d/h cost the same as one head of width d.

Think about the word "gave" in "she gave him the book". To understand it, you need three different words. Who gave? "she". Gave to whom? "him". Gave what? "book". These are three different questions.

A single head has one softmax, and one softmax has one hundred percent to share. If it spreads its weight over "she", "him" and "book", its output is a blend of all three values: a bit of the giver, a bit of the receiver, a bit of the thing given, and none of them clearly.

Multi-head attention runs several attention computations side by side. Each head has its own query, key and value matrices, so each head asks its own question and gets its own softmax. One head can put nearly all its weight on "she", another on "him", another on "book". Their outputs are laid end to end, not averaged, so the answers stay in separate parts of the vector. One more matrix, W_O, then mixes them. W_O is learned, like W_Q, W_K and W_V. Without it, each head's answer would stay in its own part of the vector and never be combined. It also brings the vector back to d numbers, the same size as the input.

Splitting into heads does not add weights. The heads are cut from the same matrices: eight heads of sixty-four numbers each, together, use exactly the weights of one head of five hundred and twelve. So more heads cost nothing extra in parameters.

What do real heads learn? In trained models, different heads really do settle on different jobs: one looks at the previous word, another links a pronoun to its noun, another follows the structure of the sentence. But be careful with the tidy story. Many heads do nothing that has a clean name, and the jobs are discovered by training, not assigned. After a worked example, we look inside the heads of a real model.

Attention Scores per Head

the cat sat: the scores for sat, split into two heads

From the attention example: 𝐪sat = [2.0, 1.4], and the keys below. Head 1 uses the first number of each vector, head 2 the second. One head uses both numbers, and divides by √2.

word key k head 1: 2.0 × k₁ head 2: 1.4 × k₂ one head: sum ÷ √2
the [0.3, 0.4] 2.0 × 0.3 = 0.60 1.4 × 0.4 = 0.56 (0.60 + 0.56) ÷ 1.41 = 0.82
cat [1.3, −0.8] 2.0 × 1.3 = 2.60 1.4 × (−0.8) = −1.12 (2.60 − 1.12) ÷ 1.41 = 1.05
sat [0.4, −1.4] 2.0 × 0.4 = 0.80 1.4 × (−1.4) = −1.96 (0.80 − 1.96) ÷ 1.41 = −0.82

A dot product adds up number by number, so one head's score is head 1's score plus head 2's score.
Head 1 scores "cat" highest; head 2 scores "the" highest.

Here is the same idea with numbers, on the three-word example from attention: "the cat sat", and the scores for "sat".

The query of "sat" is two, one point four, and the keys are in the second column. To split into two heads, give each head one of the two numbers. Head one uses only the first number of the query and of every key. Head two uses only the second.

Start with head one. Its query is 2.0. Multiply it by the first number of each key: 2.0 times 0.3 is 0.60 for "the", 2.0 times 1.3 is 2.60 for "cat", and 2.0 times 0.4 is 0.80 for "sat". Head one gives "cat" the highest score.

Head two. Its query is 1.4. Multiply it by the second number of each key: 0.56 for "the", minus 1.12 for "cat", minus 1.96 for "sat". Head two gives "the" the highest score.

Now the single head from before, which uses both numbers at once. A dot product adds up number by number, so its score for "the" is 0.60 plus 0.56: exactly head one's score plus head two's score. The same happens for every word. Its keys have two numbers, so it divides by the square root of two: 0.82, 1.05 and minus 0.82.

Notice that nothing was added: two heads of one number use exactly the same matrices as one head of two numbers. Each small head has one number, so it divides by the square root of one, which changes nothing.

Softmax per Head

each head runs its own softmax over its own scores

head 1 head 2 one head
scores for the, cat, sat 0.60, 2.60, 0.80 0.56, −1.12, −1.96 0.82, 1.05, −0.82
e^score 1.82, 13.46, 2.23 1.75, 0.33, 0.14 2.27, 2.85, 0.44
total 17.51 2.22 5.56
attention weights: e^score ÷ total 0.10, 0.77, 0.13 0.79, 0.15, 0.06 0.41, 0.51, 0.08

One head adds the two heads' scores, so "cat" and "the" share one softmax: 0.51 and 0.41.
Split into two heads, each picks one word: head 1 "cat", head 2 "the".

Now turn the scores into attention weights. Each head does this on its own, with its own softmax.

Head one: raise e to each score. e to the 0.60 is 1.82, e to the 2.60 is 13.46, e to the 0.80 is 2.23. They add up to 17.51. Divide each by the total: 0.10 for "the", 0.77 for "cat", 0.13 for "sat". Head one looks mostly at "cat".

Head two, the same way: 1.75, 0.33 and 0.14, total 2.22, so 0.79 for "the", 0.15 for "cat", 0.06 for "sat". Head two looks mostly at "the".

The single head: 2.27, 2.85 and 0.44, total 5.56, so 0.41 for "the", 0.51 for "cat", and 0.08 for "sat".

So one head mixes the two heads together. Head one prefers "cat", head two prefers "the", and adding their scores blurs the two preferences into one softmax that splits its weight between them. With two heads, each preference gets its own softmax, and each head can pick one word.

Every head has an attention weight for all three words; what changes is how the weight is spread.

Attention Heads in a Trained Model

a small GPT trained on Tang poems: its four first-block heads, reading 床前明月光，疑是地上霜。

All four heads look a fixed distance back — possible only because positions are in the vectors.
Head 4 looks at the character directly above the next one: before writing 霜, it looks at 光.

From here on, our running example is a real model rather than the two-number toy. It is a small GPT trained on Tang poems. It reads one Chinese character at a time, knows 7,349 characters, looks back at most 64 characters, and gives each character 256 numbers, with four heads of sixty-four. The toy is too small for what follows: normalizing a vector of two numbers, which we will do soon, leaves nothing but plus one and minus one.

Before building the rest of the model, look at what attention actually learned in this one, because it answers the question from multi-head attention: do different heads really do different things?

Each square is one weight. Rows are the character doing the looking — the query — and columns are the characters it can look at. The mask is why everything above the diagonal is empty.

Every head in the first block has settled on a simple rule. Head one looks at the character itself. Head three looks two characters back. Head two looks four back. And head four looks exactly five characters back — at all fifty-seven positions we tested, across three different poems. None of these rules was given to the model. They came out of training, and none of them would be possible without the position vectors from the start of this lecture, since a head that looks "five back" has to know where things are.

Why five? A line is five characters and a punctuation mark, so six positions. Standing at 上 and about to write the next character, five back is 光: the character directly above the one being written, at the same place in the line before. In Tang poetry the two lines of a couplet match up position by position, and the last characters of the second and fourth lines rhyme. So when the model is about to write 霜, head four is looking at 光. 光 and 霜 rhyme.

This is the first block, where heads are simple. Heads in later blocks spread their weight much more and have no rule this clean, which is the normal situation in large models too.

Position-Wise Feed-Forward Network

FFN(𝐱)=W2GELU(W1𝐱+𝐛1)+𝐛2
GELU(x)=x·Φ(x),Φ(x)=P(Z≤x)=∫−∞xφ(t)dt,φ(t)=12πe−t2/2,Z~𝒩(0,1)
  x               -2      -1       0       1       2
  Φ(x)          0.02    0.16    0.50    0.84    0.98
  GELU(x)      -0.05   -0.16       0    0.84    1.95   x · Φ(x)
  ReLU(x)          0       0       0       1       2   x · (0 or 1)
  GELU slope   -0.09   -0.08    0.50    1.08    1.09   Φ(x) + x · φ(x)
  ReLU slope       0       0       -       1       1

Why an FFN: attention only mixes (a weighted sum). The FFN computes on each position alone, with the same weights.
Why GELU: ReLU's slope is 0 for every negative x, so no gradient flows back there; GELU's is not, and it trains slightly better.

Attention is the only part of a transformer where words exchange information. Each word ends up with a weighted sum of what the others passed on. But a weighted sum is just mixing. Something still has to compute with the result.

That is the job of the second part of every block, and you have already built it: a layer, a bend, and another layer. The neural language model we built had exactly this shape. Here it takes a character's 256 numbers, widens them to 1,024 with the first matrix, bends them with GELU, and narrows them back to 256 with the second.

GELU is the bend, and it is easiest to understand next to ReLU. ReLU multiplies x by either 0 or 1: by 1 if x is positive, by 0 if it is not. GELU multiplies x by a number between 0 and 1 instead, and that number is Phi of x.

Phi of x is a probability. Take a random number Z from the standard normal distribution, the bell curve with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Phi of x is the chance that Z is less than or equal to x. For a very negative x, that chance is close to 0. At x equal to 0 it is exactly one half, because the bell curve is symmetric. For a large positive x it is close to 1. The integral on the slide is the area under the bell curve to the left of x.

Now read the table. At x equal to 2, Phi is 0.98, so GELU gives 2 times 0.98, which is 1.95: almost the same as ReLU's 2. At x equal to minus 2, Phi is 0.02, so GELU gives minus 0.05: almost the same as ReLU's 0. The difference is near zero. ReLU jumps from multiplying by 0 to multiplying by 1 exactly at zero. GELU changes the multiplier gradually, so at x equal to minus 1 it still multiplies by 0.16 and gives minus 0.16.

Why use GELU at all? Look at the slope rows. Training moves each weight using the slope, the gradient. ReLU's slope is exactly 0 for every negative x, so when a neuron's input is negative, nothing flows back and its weights get no update from that example. If its input is negative for every example, it never learns again. GELU's slope is Phi of x plus x times phi of x, where phi is the bell curve itself. It is not 0 for negative x, about minus 0.08 at x equal to minus 1, so some gradient always flows back. In experiments, GELU trained slightly better than ReLU, and GPT-2 and BERT adopted it. That measurement, not a proof, is the real reason.

"Position-wise" means it is applied to each position separately, with the same weights, and positions do not talk to each other inside it. So a block has a clear division of labor: attention gathers information from other positions, and the feed-forward network processes what each position gathered.

Widening to four times the width and back is expensive: in a transformer, the feed-forward networks hold most of each block's parameters, about twice as many as attention. Research that looks inside trained models finds that much of what a model has memorized — facts, word associations — seems to be stored in these layers.

Residual Connections

𝐱out=𝐱+f(𝐱)∂xout∂x=1+f′(x)
  toy: 4 layers, each with slope f'(x) = 0.1   (slopes multiply: chain rule)
    without residual    0.1 × 0.1 × 0.1 × 0.1                    = 0.0001
    with residual       (1 + 0.1) × (1 + 0.1) × (1 + 0.1) × (1 + 0.1) = 1.46
  the vector for 上 in 床前明月光，疑是地上 — its length, block by block
  block   arriving   attention adds   feed-forward adds   leaving
    1        1.17          8.18              4.13           10.38
    2       10.38          3.96              4.56           13.21
    3       13.21          6.26              6.63           17.87
    4       17.87          9.10              6.74           23.86

Why: the gradient at an early layer is a product of one slope per layer; small slopes multiplied together vanish.
With 𝐱+f(𝐱), each factor is 1 + (slope of f), so the 1 carries the gradient back.

Each sublayer in a block — attention, then the feed-forward network — is wrapped in the same simple rule. The output is not f of x. It is x plus f of x. The input goes around the sublayer and is added back to what the sublayer produced. That route around is called a residual connection, or a skip connection.

The table follows one real vector through the model: the character 上, at the end of our input. It arrives at block one with a length of about one point two. Attention adds a correction of length about eight, the feed-forward network adds about four, and it leaves at about ten. Then the next block adds its own corrections on top, and so on, until it leaves the last block at about twenty-four. Think of it as one running vector that every sublayer reads from and writes a small addition to. People call it the residual stream.

Why build it this way? Remember vanishing gradients. The slope reaching an early layer is a product of one factor per layer, and a long product runs away. The toy at the top shows it. Four layers, each with slope 0.1: without residual connections the gradient is 0.1 multiplied four times, 0.0001, and the first layer barely learns. With a residual connection the output is x plus f of x, so each factor is one plus 0.1, and the product is 1.46. Even if the sublayer's own slope is tiny, the one is still there. The gradient always has a route straight back through the additions, all the way to the embeddings, without passing through a single layer's multiplication. This is the fix promised when we met vanishing gradients, and it is what lets people stack a hundred blocks and still train them.

It also makes a fresh block harmless. At the start of training, when a sublayer knows nothing, it adds a small correction and the vector passes through almost unchanged. The model begins close to "do nothing" and learns what to add.

Layer Normalization

LN(𝐱)=γ⊙𝐱−μσ2+ϵ+β,μ=1d∑i=1dxi,σ2=1d∑i=1d(xi−μ)2
  toy   x = [1, 3, 5, 7]   μ = 4   σ = 2.24   (x − μ)/σ = [-1.34 -0.45 0.45 1.34]

  post-LN  (2017)      x = LN( x + f(x) )     normalize the stream itself
  pre-LN   (GPT-2 on)  x = x + f( LN(x) )     normalize only what f reads

Why: the residual stream keeps growing (上: length 1.17 into block 1, 23.86 out of block 4), so each sublayer would see numbers of a different size.
LN gives every sublayer mean 0 and spread 1, then learned γ, β. Pre-LN keeps the residual path clean.

The residual stream keeps growing. On the last slide, the vector for 上 had length 1.17 going into block one and 23.86 coming out of block four. If each sublayer received numbers of a different size, each would have to be tuned to its own scale, and a deep stack would be fragile to train. Layer normalization removes that problem.

It works on one vector at a time. Take its d numbers, subtract their mean, mu, and divide by their spread, sigma, the standard deviation. The small epsilon only stops a division by zero. The toy line shows it on four numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7 have mean 4 and standard deviation the square root of 5, about 2.24, so they become minus 1.34, minus 0.45, 0.45 and 1.34. The result always has mean zero and spread one, whatever came in. Then each coordinate is multiplied by a learned scale, gamma, and shifted by a learned bias, beta, so the model can still choose a different size where it helps.

Where to put it turned out to matter. The original 2017 transformer normalized after the addition: the whole stream went through LayerNorm at every block. Since GPT-2, almost every model normalizes before the sublayer instead: f reads a normalized copy, and its output is added to the stream, which itself is never normalized on the way up. This model does it that way.

Why did pre-LN win? Look at the residual path. In pre-LN it is pure addition from the bottom of the model to the top, so the gradient's route straight back — the one from the previous slide — is left completely clean. In post-LN every block puts a normalization on that route. Post-LN models can be trained, but they need a very careful learning-rate warm-up and become unstable as they get deeper. Pre-LN models train reliably at depth, and a single extra LayerNorm is added after the last block.

The Transformer Block

the whole block, as written in the model's own training code

𝐱←𝐱+MultiHead(LN1(𝐱))
𝐱←𝐱+FFN(LN2(𝐱))
def forward(s, x):
    B, t, _ = x.shape
    q, k, v = s.qkv(s.ln1(x)).split(C, 2)              # LN, then W_Q W_K W_V
    q, k, v = (z.view(B, t, H, C // H).transpose(1, 2)  # split into 4 heads
               for z in (q, k, v))
    a = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(C // H)   # scores / sqrt(d_k)
    a = a.masked_fill(~s.mask[:t, :t], float("-inf")).softmax(-1)
    x = x + s.drop(s.proj((a @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, t, C)))
    return x + s.drop(s.mlp(s.ln2(x)))                  # LN, FFN, add

Two lines of mathematics, nine lines of code. Every piece has already been built.
The block's output has the same shape as its input, so blocks can be stacked.

Here is everything so far, assembled. As mathematics, a transformer block is two lines. Normalise the stream, run multi-head attention on it, and add the result back. Then normalise again, run the feed-forward network, and add that back.

Below it is the block from the training code of the poem model, and every line is something we have built. Line three normalises and makes the queries, keys and values in one matrix product. Line four splits them into four heads of sixty-four numbers each. Line six is the scores, divided by the square root of sixty-four. Line seven is the causal mask and the softmax. Line eight takes the weighted sum of values, joins the heads back together, applies the output matrix, and adds the result to the stream: the residual connection. The last line is the second half: normalise, feed-forward network, add. The word "drop" is dropout, which randomly zeroes a few numbers during training to prevent memorising, and does nothing when the model is used.

Two things to notice. The first is how short it is. The mechanism behind every large language model fits in a few lines, and you can now read every one of them.

The second is the shape. A vector of 256 numbers per position goes in, and a vector of 256 numbers per position comes out. That is what lets blocks be stacked: the output of one block is a perfectly good input to the next. Stacking them is the next slide.

A Decoder-Only Transformer

flowchart LR
    C["characters<br/>春眠不覺"] --> X["E[w] + P[t]<br/>256 numbers each"]
    X --> B["4 × block<br/>attention + FFN"]
    B --> N["final LN"]
    N --> S["output layer<br/>7,349 scores"]
    S --> P["softmax<br/>P(next)"]

  春眠不覺 ->   睡 0.099   曉 0.071   春 0.033   夜 0.023   月 0.022

  24 characters generated, one at a time:
  高樓倚一望，遠客望三湘。白日蒼蒼玉，清風吹紫華。

Only the middle changed. The lookup, the scores, the softmax and the loss are those of the neural language model.
Trained on next-character prediction with cross-entropy; the output layer reuses E.

Stack the blocks and put the parts we already know on either end, and you have the complete model.

Characters come in and become ids. Each id picks up a row of the embedding table, and its position's row is added. The vectors pass through four transformer blocks. A final LayerNorm, then an output layer with one score for each of the 7,349 characters, then softmax. The model is trained exactly like the neural language model we built earlier: at every position, minus the log of the probability given to the character that really came next, averaged over the text.

Compare this with that earlier model. The front is the same: an embedding lookup. The back is the same: scores for every token, softmax, cross-entropy. Only the middle has changed. Where there was one layer reading a fixed window of two words laid end to end, there are now four blocks of attention and feed-forward networks, reading up to sixty-four characters with the same weights at every position.

Run it. Given 春眠不覺, the model gives 睡 about ten percent and 曉 — the real next character in the famous poem — about seven percent. For a model with five million parameters that is reasonable: both fit. And generating is just this, repeated: pick a character from the probabilities, add it to the input, run the model again. The couplets on the slide were written that way, twenty-four characters, one at a time. They have the right shape — five characters, a comma, five characters, a full stop — and the words fit the genre, even though the poem does not quite make sense.

This design, with only the masked decoder blocks, is called decoder-only. GPT-2, GPT-3, Llama, Qwen, and nearly every chat model you use are this shape, just with more blocks and wider vectors. If you look back at the diagram from the original paper in the first lecture, you can now read every box in its right-hand half.

Parameter Count of a Transformer

GPT-2 small: vocabulary |V| = 50,257, context T = 1,024, width d = 768, L = 12 blocks

one block=4d2+4d⏟attention+8d2+5d⏟feed-forward+4d⏟2 LayerNorms=12d2+13d≈12d2
GPT-2 small shape parameters share
E token embedding (also the output layer) |V|×d 38,597,376 31.0%
P position embedding T×d 786,432 0.6%
attention: four d×d matrices and biases L×(4d2+4d) 28,348,416 22.8%
feed-forward: W1 (4d×d), W2 (d×4d), biases L×(8d2+5d) 56,669,184 45.5%
LayerNorms: γ,β L×4d+2d 38,400 0.03%
total 124,439,808

Why count: parameters decide how much memory a model needs and what it costs to run.
All blocks ≈12Ld2: GPT-2 small 84.9M (exact 85.1M); GPT-3, L = 96, d = 12,288: 174B (published 175B).

Count what is inside a real model, the same way we counted the neural language model. Take GPT-2 small: a vocabulary of 50,257 tokens, a context of 1,024, vectors of 768 numbers, and 12 blocks.

Start with one block. Attention has four matrices, W_Q, W_K, W_V and W_O, each d by d, plus a bias of d numbers for each: four d squared plus four d. The feed-forward network has W_1, 4d by d, with a bias of 4d, and W_2, d by 4d, with a bias of d: eight d squared plus five d. Each LayerNorm has a gamma and a beta of d numbers, and there are two per block: four d. Added up, one block is twelve d squared plus thirteen d. When d is 768, the twelve d squared part is almost all of it.

Now the whole model. The embedding table is 50,257 times 768, about 38.6 million. It is used twice, once to look up the input and again as the output layer, but it is stored once, so it is counted once. The position table is 1,024 times 768. Then twelve blocks, and one final LayerNorm. The total is 124,439,808, which is exactly the published size of GPT-2 small.

The rule to remember is twelve L d squared for the blocks. For GPT-2 small it gives 84.9 million, against an exact 85.1 million. For GPT-3, with 96 blocks of width 12,288, it gives about 174 billion, and GPT-3 is published as 175 billion. So one short formula tells you where size comes from. Parameters grow with the square of the width: double d and every block costs four times as much. Add blocks and the cost grows in proportion.

Notice also what is almost missing from the count: the context length. It appears only in the position table, less than one percent here. A model that reads a thousand tokens and one that reads a hundred thousand can have almost the same number of parameters. Longer context costs memory and compute when the model runs, not weights.

The Transformer, End to End

flowchart BT
    T["tokens"] --> EP["E[w] + P[t]"]
    EP --> B["one block, repeated L times
x + MultiHead(LN(x))
x + FFN(LN(x))"]
    B --> O["LN, output layer, softmax"]

Attention moves information between positions; the feed-forward network computes on each.
Residuals and LayerNorm make a deep stack trainable.

Here is the whole model once more, on one line.

Tokens become vectors, with their positions added so that order is in the numbers. Then a block, repeated L times. In the first half of the block, attention lets every position gather information from the positions before it. In the second half, a feed-forward network computes on each position alone. Both halves read a normalized copy of the stream and add their result back to it. After the last block, a final LayerNorm, an output layer, and softmax give a probability for every token.

Three things to take away.

First, each piece exists to solve a specific problem. Positional embeddings, because attention cannot see order. The feed-forward network, because a weighted sum is only mixing. Residual connections, because gradients vanish in deep stacks. LayerNorm, because the stream grows.

Second, you can now read the real thing. The block is nine lines of code, and every line is something you have computed.

Third, the model that writes Tang couplets and GPT-2 are the same architecture. The difference between them is width, depth, vocabulary and the amount of text they were trained on — which is where the story of large language models goes next.
